question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Amiss
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Impeccable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Amiss means: wrong, faulty, out of order, improper — something not quite right. (कुछ गड़बड़/दोषपूर्ण)
◦ Example: There's something amiss with the printer; it keeps jamming.

• Impeccable means: flawless, faultless, without any mistake or blemish. (त्रुटिरहित/निर्दोष)
◦ Example: Her manners were impeccable.

• Since "amiss" denotes a fault or defect, its exact opposite is "impeccable", which denotes the complete absence of any fault.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Marred (बिगड़ा हुआ): means spoiled or damaged — this is close in meaning to "amiss", not its opposite.

• Option 3: Gaily (उल्लासपूर्वक): means in a cheerful, lively manner — unrelated to the idea of correctness or fault.

• Option 4: Vitiated (दूषित): means spoiled, corrupted, or made legally invalid — this is also a synonym-like word, not an opposite.

NOTE

• Other words close in meaning to "amiss": awry, faulty, defective, improper.

• Other synonyms of "impeccable": flawless, immaculate, unblemished, perfect.

• Common SSC antonym pairs: amiss x impeccable, flaw x perfection.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.
A study finds that the average staff cost at a public sector bank is high than that at its
private sector counterpart.
option_3: a public sector bank is high than that at
option_4: A study finds that the average staff cost at
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. a public sector bank is high than that at.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: When two things are compared using "than", the adjective or adverb before it must be in the comparative degree (e.g., higher, better, more). A positive-degree adjective like "high" cannot be directly followed by "than".

• The given sentence compares "the average staff cost at a public sector bank" with "that at its private sector counterpart" using "than", so the adjective "high" must change to the comparative "higher".

• The erroneous segment is: "a public sector bank is high than that at" — it should read "a public sector bank is higher than that at".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because a clear comparative-degree error exists, as explained above.

• Option 2: "its private sector counterpart." is grammatically correct as it stands.

• Option 4: "A study finds that the average staff cost at" is grammatically correct — the present tense "finds" correctly reports a general/habitual finding.

NOTE

• Degrees of comparison: Positive + as...as; Comparative + than; Superlative + the...est/most.

• Common SSC error: "senior than" (should be "senior to"), "superior than" (should be "superior to") — these Latin-origin comparatives take "to", not "than".

• Regular comparative pattern for one-syllable adjectives: high → higher → highest (add -er/-est).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Prunke.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Prunke" is not a correctly spelled English word; the intended word is "Prune" — meaning a dried plum, or (as a verb) to trim or cut back a plant.
◦ Example: She pruned the rose bushes before winter.

• The other three options — Hinder, Sober, Tension — are all correctly spelled.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hinder" — correctly spelled; means to obstruct or delay.

• Option 2: "Sober" — correctly spelled; means not drunk, or serious and calm in manner.

• Option 4: "Tension" — correctly spelled; means a state of mental strain or nervousness.

NOTE

• Commonly confused spellings tested by SSC: "Pronunciation" (not "Pronounciation"), "Embarrass" (double r, double s), "Occurrence" (double c, double r).

• Silent letters and doubled consonants are the most frequent trap in SSC spelling questions.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: Fine fthers do not make fine birds.
option_2: Figne feathers do not make fine brds.
option_3: Fine fathears do not make fine birds.
option_4: Fine feathers do not make fine birds.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Fine feathers do not make fine birds.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 4 contains no spelling errors — every word (Fine, feathers, do, not, make, fine, birds) is correctly spelled.

• The other three options each contain at least one misspelled word: "fthers", "figne", "brds", "fathears".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect: "fthers" should be "feathers" (the letters "ea" are missing).

• Option 2 is incorrect: "Figne" should be "Fine" and "brds" should be "birds".

• Option 3 is incorrect: "fathears" should be "feathers".

NOTE

• This line is based on the well-known proverb "Fine feathers make fine birds", meaning that outward appearance or dress affects how a person is judged.

• In SSC spelling questions, always read every word letter-by-letter; errors are usually a single missing, extra, or transposed letter.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if
the sentence is grammatically correct.
Fashion is not something that exists in dresses only.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined portion "that exists in" is grammatically correct as it stands: "something" (singular, third person) correctly takes the singular present-tense verb "exists", and the relative pronoun "that" correctly refers back to "something".

• None of the alternatives improve upon this — each one introduces a fresh grammatical error (see below).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "that exist of" is incorrect: "exist" does not agree with the singular subject "something" (it should be "exists"), and "of" is the wrong preposition after "exist" (it should be "in").

• Option 2: "that existing at" is incorrect: "existing" is a participle and cannot function as the main verb after "that" in this construction; also "at" is the wrong preposition.

• Option 4: "which exist on" is incorrect: subject-verb agreement is wrong ("exist" instead of "exists"), and "on" is the wrong preposition (it should be "in").

NOTE

• Subject-verb agreement rule: a singular indefinite pronoun like "something", "someone", "anything" always takes a singular verb.

• Common SSC trap: mixing up prepositions like in/on/at/of after common verbs — always check the exact preposition that idiomatically follows the verb ("exists in", not "exists of/on/at").

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Worried
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Unconcerned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Worried means: anxious or troubled about actual or potential problems. (चिंतित)
◦ Example: She was worried about her exam results.

• Unconcerned means: not feeling or showing worry or interest; indifferent. (निश्चिंत/उदासीन)
◦ Example: He remained unconcerned even after hearing the bad news.

• Since "worried" denotes anxiety, its exact opposite is "unconcerned" — free from anxiety or worry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Leisure (अवकाश): means free time; a noun unrelated in sense to "worried".

• Option 2: Withdraw (हटना/वापस लेना): means to remove oneself or take something back; unrelated to worry.

• Option 3: Proceed (आगे बढ़ना): means to go forward or continue; unrelated to worry.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "worried": anxious, troubled, uneasy, apprehensive.

• Other antonyms of "worried": calm, relaxed, carefree, composed.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. to focus more on edible oils/oilseeds than on wheat
Q. the MSP for wheat is up by 2 per cent while
R. that of rapeseed-mustard is up by 8.6 per cent,
S. perhaps indicating that the government wants
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. QRSP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Q begins with the main clause subject, "the MSP for wheat is up by 2 per cent while" — a natural sentence-opener that introduces a contrast using "while".

• R continues the contrast: "that of rapeseed-mustard is up by 8.6 per cent," — here "that" refers back to "the MSP" in Q, so R must directly follow Q.

• S follows with the inference: "perhaps indicating that the government wants" — this logically follows once the comparative facts in Q and R have been stated.

• P completes the sentence, stating what the government wants: "to focus more on edible oils/oilseeds than on wheat" — it grammatically completes the infinitive begun in S ("wants to focus...").

• Full sentence: "The MSP for wheat is up by 2 per cent while that of rapeseed-mustard is up by 8.6 per cent, perhaps indicating that the government wants to focus more on edible oils/oilseeds than on wheat."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (QRSP).

Additional Information

• Option 2: RSPQ is incorrect: R begins with "that of rapeseed-mustard", but "that" needs an antecedent ("the MSP") which has not yet been introduced.

• Option 3: PSRQ is incorrect: P begins with an infinitive "to focus...", which cannot start a standalone sentence without a preceding subject and verb.

• Option 4: PRQS is incorrect: the same problem applies — P cannot open the sentence, and the logical cause-effect chain (percentages first, then inference) is broken.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions, look for a "starter" part that can stand independently (a clear subject + verb, no dangling pronoun/reference) — here Q is the only such part.

• Words like "that", "this", "it", "while", "perhaps indicating" are strong linking clues — "that of rapeseed-mustard" must refer to something already named (MSP), and "indicating" naturally follows factual data.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative
which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
A bull market
option_2: A market where cattle is traded
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Market where prices are rising.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A bull market" means a financial market in which share or asset prices are rising, or are expected to rise. (वह बाज़ार जिसमें कीमतें बढ़ रही हों)
◦ Example: Investors were confident during the bull market of the early 2000s.

• The term comes from the way a bull attacks — thrusting its horns upward — symbolising rising prices.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: A fertile field (उपजाऊ खेत): refers to fertile agricultural land, unrelated to financial markets.

• Option 2: A market where cattle is traded: a literal, non-idiomatic misreading of "bull"; not the idiomatic meaning.

• Option 3: To boast (डींग मारना): closer to unrelated slang usage of "bull"; not the meaning of "bull market".

NOTE

• The opposite idiom is "A bear market" — a market in which prices are falling (a bear strikes downward with its paws).

• Other stock-market idioms tested by SSC: "blue chip" (a reliable, financially sound company), "on a roll" (a run of continued success).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
We won an unprecedented pardon from ______ -President Karzai, and Gulnaz was
freed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. then.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "then" used before a designation or title (as in "then-President", "then-Prime Minister") means "at that particular time" and correctly modifies "President Karzai" to show he held that position at the time referred to.

• "then-President Karzai" is a standard fixed usage meaning "the person who was President at that time, Karzai".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "those" is incorrect: it is a plural demonstrative and cannot modify a singular title like "President Karzai".

• Option 3: "at time" is incorrect: this is not idiomatic English (the correct phrase would be "at the time"), and even so it does not fit grammatically before a title.

• Option 4: "later" is incorrect: "later" means "after this time / afterward", which contradicts the required sense of "at that time".

NOTE

• "then" as a time-adjective is hyphenated before a noun/title in formal writing: "the then-Prime Minister", "the then-government".

• Common SSC trap: confusing "then" (time adjective, "at that time") with "than" (used in comparisons).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
The makers of sports drinks spend tens to hundreds of millions of dollars ______ their
products each year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. advertising.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes sports-drink makers spending huge sums of money each year — the logical, correctly-collocated verb after "spend...dollars" in this context is "advertising", meaning to promote their products to increase sales.

• "Spend money advertising something" is a common and correct collocation in English.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "snacking" means eating light food between meals — has no logical connection with spending money on products.

• Option 2: "lingering" means staying somewhere longer than necessary — does not fit the context of spending money on products.

• Option 3: "varying" means changing or making different — does not logically complete the sentence about spending money each year.

NOTE

• Common SSC collocations: "spend money on/doing something", "invest in something", "spend time doing something".

• Related word forms: advertise (verb), advertisement (noun), advertiser (noun), advertising (gerund/noun).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Despondent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Hopeful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Despondent means: in low spirits from loss of hope or courage; dejected, discouraged. (निराश)
◦ Example: He felt despondent after failing the interview for the third time.

• Hopeful means: feeling or inspiring optimism about a future event; full of hope. (आशान्वित)
◦ Example: She remained hopeful of clearing the exam despite the setback.

• Since "despondent" denotes hopelessness, its exact opposite is "hopeful".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Precise (सटीक): means exact and accurate; unrelated to hope or despair.

• Option 2: Despaired: a form related to "despair", i.e. close in meaning to "despondent", not its opposite.

• Option 3: Reproach (निंदा करना): means to express disapproval or criticism; unrelated to hope or despair.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "despondent": dejected, downcast, disheartened, gloomy.

• Other antonyms of "despondent": optimistic, cheerful, buoyant, upbeat.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose
‘No error’.
In the five next years, the migration will surely stop.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In the five next.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: When both a number (five) and an ordering word like "next"/"last" modify a noun (years), the standard English word order is: "next/last + number + noun", i.e. "the next five years", NOT "the five next years".

• The segment "In the five next" reverses this correct order and is therefore the error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because the word-order error described above does exist.

• Option 2: "will surely stop." is grammatically correct.

• Option 4: "years, the migration" is grammatically correct as part of the sentence.

NOTE

• Correct pattern: "the next five years", "the last three days", "the first two chapters" — the ordering word always comes before the number.

• Common SSC trap: reversed word order with determiners like "next", "last", "first", "other" placed before numerals.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
I ______ pay too much attention to the stories.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. didn't.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The auxiliary "did" (past tense) is used with the base form of the main verb (V1) in negative sentences: Subject + did not/didn't + V1.

• Here the main verb given is "pay" (base form), so the correct auxiliary is "didn't" — "I didn't pay too much attention to the stories."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hasn't" is incorrect: "hasn't" is used with a past participle (V3) — "hasn't paid", not the base form "pay".

• Option 3: "wasn't" is incorrect: "wasn't" is used with a present participle for the continuous tense ("wasn't paying"), not directly before "pay".

• Option 4: "haven't" is incorrect: "haven't" is used with a past participle (V3) — "haven't paid", not the base form "pay".

NOTE

• Tense-auxiliary agreement: did + V1 (simple past negative); has/have + V3 (present perfect negative); was/were + V-ing (past continuous negative).

• Common SSC trap: choosing an auxiliary that doesn't match the form of the main verb already given in the sentence.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Ponderous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Heavy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ponderous means: (of an object) very heavy and awkward to move or use; also (of speech/style) dull, laborious, or slow-moving. (भारी-भरकम)
◦ Example: The ponderous old wardrobe took four men to lift.

• Heavy is the closest synonym, referring directly to great weight or mass.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Unruly (उद्दंड/अनियंत्रित): means disorderly or difficult to control; unrelated to weight.

• Option 2: Wondrous (अद्भुत): means inspiring wonder or awe; unrelated to weight.

• Option 3: Bluff (रूखा/सीधा-सादा): means blunt and hearty in manner, or a steep cliff; unrelated to weight.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "ponderous": weighty, cumbersome, hefty, bulky.

• "Ponderous" can also describe writing or speech that is dull and overly serious — a secondary meaning often tested in reading passages.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One who offers one's services without being forced
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Volunteer.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Volunteer" is a person who offers to do something, especially a service, of their own free will, without being forced or paid. (स्वेच्छा से सेवा देने वाला व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: Hundreds of volunteers helped distribute relief material after the flood.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Skeptic (संशयवादी): a person who doubts accepted beliefs; unrelated to offering services.

• Option 2: Altruist (परोपकारी): a person who is unselfishly concerned for the well-being of others; close in spirit, but this describes a general selfless disposition, not specifically "offering services without being forced".

• Option 4: Scholar (विद्वान): a person of great learning; unrelated to offering services.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Volunteer" with "Altruist": an altruist acts selflessly for others' welfare in general, while a volunteer specifically offers unpaid service or help.

• Other common one-word substitution: "Philanthropist" — one who works for the welfare of others, especially through donating money.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative
which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Take your eye off the ball
option_1: To stop paying attention for a moment
option_3: Take an advice from a wrong person
option_4: Deteriorating and headed for complete disaster
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To stop paying attention for a moment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Take your eye off the ball" means to stop concentrating on something important, even briefly, and as a result make a mistake or miss an opportunity. (थोड़े समय के लिए ध्यान भटक जाना)
◦ Example: The company took its eye off the ball for a moment and a rival launched a similar product first.

• It comes from sports (like cricket/tennis) where a player must keep watching the ball closely to play it well.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Take someone for grated" (correctly "take for granted" — फालतू में लेना/महत्व न देना) means to fail to appreciate someone; a different idiom altogether.

• Option 3: "Take an advice from a wrong person" is not a recognised idiom matching this phrase; it is a literal description unrelated to "eye off the ball".

• Option 4: "Deteriorating and headed for complete disaster" describes an idiom like "going from bad to worse" or "spiralling out of control", not "take your eye off the ball".

NOTE

• Related idiom: "Keep your eye on the ball" — the opposite, meaning to stay focused and alert.

• Other focus-related idioms: "lose sight of" (to forget about something important), "keep tabs on" (to monitor closely).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
The extremists have assassinated the President.
option_1: The President has been assassinated by the extremists.
option_2: The President had been assassinated by the extremists.
option_3: The President is assassinated by the extremists.
option_4: The President was assassinated by the extremists.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The President has been assassinated by the extremists.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The extremists have assassinated the President" is in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the President" becomes the subject; since it is third person singular, the auxiliary is "has"; "been" is added; the verb "assassinated" (already V3) is retained; and "the extremists" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The President has been assassinated by the extremists.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had been" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense used in the active sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is" (Simple Present passive) does not correspond to the "have + V3" structure of the active sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was" is the passive of the Simple Past Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• Present Perfect passive formula: has/have + been + V3.

• Common SSC trap: the tense of the passive auxiliary must correspond exactly to the tense of the active sentence — the number of "helping verbs" used in the active and passive forms of Perfect tenses must match.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Illusions are usually related with ______ processes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. visual.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Visual" means relating to seeing or sight. Illusions (e.g., optical illusions) are most commonly associated with what we see, i.e., visual perception.

• Hence "visual processes" is the most contextually and logically appropriate completion of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "audio" relates to hearing/sound, not the sense typically associated with the word "illusion" in general usage.

• Option 3: "oratory" relates to public speaking; unrelated to the perceptual context of illusions.

• Option 4: "digital" relates to computers/technology; unrelated to the perceptual/sensory context implied here.

NOTE

• Common SSC vocabulary trap: choosing a word that is topically related but does not collocate correctly with the rest of the sentence — always check which word most naturally "goes with" the subject (here, "illusions" naturally pairs with "visual").

• Word family: vision (noun), visualize (verb), visible (adjective), visually (adverb).

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
The father said to his daughter, “Your mother will be waiting for me.”
option_1: The father told his daughter that her mother was waiting for me.
option_2: The father told his daughter that her mother would be waiting for him.
option_3: The father told his daughter that my mother would be waiting for him.
option_4: The father told his daughter that her mother will be waiting for him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The father told his daughter that her mother would be waiting for him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Direct to Indirect Speech (statement with future tense "will"):
◦ The reporting verb "said to" changes to "told" (since it has an object, "his daughter").
◦ The comma and quotation marks are removed and replaced with the conjunction "that".
◦ Tense change: "will" (future) changes to "would", since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense.
◦ Pronoun change: "Your" (referring to the daughter) changes to "her"; "me" (referring to the father) changes to "him".

• Applying the rule: "Your mother will be waiting for me" becomes "that her mother would be waiting for him".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect: "was waiting" wrongly shifts the tense to past continuous instead of "would be waiting", and "me" should have changed to "him" but was left unchanged.

• Option 3 is incorrect: the pronoun "my" is wrong — it should be "her", referring to the daughter (the person being addressed), not the speaker reporting the sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect: the tense "will" should change to "would" in indirect speech since the reporting verb "told" is in the past tense.

NOTE

• Pronoun-change rule: change pronouns according to the person being referred to, from the reporter's point of view, not the original speaker's.

• Tense-backshift rule: will → would, can → could, may → might, is/am/are → was/were, when the reporting verb is in the past tense.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A person who is indifferent to pain and pleasures of life
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Stoic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Stoic" is a person who can endure pain or hardship without showing their feelings or complaining, remaining indifferent to both pleasure and pain. (सुख-दुख में समभाव रखने वाला व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: He bore the tragic loss with stoic calm, showing no outward emotion.

• The word derives from the ancient Greek school of philosophy called Stoicism, which taught indifference to pleasure and pain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Vagabond (आवारा): a person who wanders from place to place without a home or job; unrelated to indifference to pain/pleasure.

• Option 2: Amateur (शौकिया): a person who engages in an activity for pleasure rather than as a profession; unrelated to this meaning.

• Option 4: Recluse (एकांतवासी): a person who lives a solitary life and avoids others; related to isolation, not specifically to indifference toward pain and pleasure.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Stoic" with "Recluse": a recluse avoids social contact, while a stoic remains emotionally unmoved by pain or pleasure regardless of social contact.

• Other common one-word substitution: "Cynic" — one who believes people are motivated only by self-interest.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.
First, the e-commerce industry has historically struggled with (1)______ issues. The Internet has made it possible for customers to place (2) ______ from any location, but that convenience comes with a cost in (3) ______ of shipping costs and order fulfillment times. But by hosting their e-commerce sites on cloud computing platforms, merchants can offload (4) ______ of the server processing work. These third-party systems still (5) ______ full control over the look and feel of their online stores.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. delivery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that e-commerce has "historically struggled with ___ issues", and the very next sentence talks about "shipping costs and order fulfillment times" — both of which directly relate to getting goods to customers.

• "Delivery issues" is therefore the most contextually appropriate word, referring to the well-known challenge of delivering ordered goods to customers efficiently.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "flipping" means turning something over; it does not fit the context of e-commerce challenges.

• Option 2: "placing" means putting something in position; while "placing orders" is a common phrase, "placing issues" does not make sense here.

• Option 3: "storing" relates to warehousing goods; the passage later emphasises "shipping" and "fulfillment" rather than storage, making "delivery" the closer contextual fit.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the sentences before and after the blank — the later reference to "shipping costs and order fulfillment times" is the key clue confirming "delivery" here.

• Common SSC cloze strategy: eliminate options that are grammatically valid but contextually unrelated.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.
First, the e-commerce industry has historically struggled with (1)______ issues. The Internet has made it possible for customers to place (2) ______ from any location, but that convenience comes with a cost in (3) ______ of shipping costs and order fulfillment times. But by hosting their e-commerce sites on cloud computing platforms, merchants can offload (4) ______ of the server processing work. These third-party systems still (5) ______ full control over the look and feel of their online stores.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. orders.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "place an order / place orders" is a standard, fixed collocation in English meaning "to make a request to buy something".

• "The Internet has made it possible for customers to place orders from any location" is a natural, grammatically correct, and contextually appropriate sentence about online shopping.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "systems" does not collocate with "place" in this context; one does not "place systems".

• Option 2: "series" does not collocate with "place" in this context.

• Option 3: "locals" refers to local people/residents; "place locals" does not make sense here.

NOTE

• Common e-commerce collocations: "place an order", "track a shipment", "process a payment", "browse a catalogue".

• Cloze passages frequently test fixed verb-noun collocations like "place + order" — memorising common collocations helps eliminate wrong options quickly.

The Internet has made it possible for customers to place (2) ______ from any location, but that convenience comes with a cost in (3) ______ of shipping costs and order fulfillment times. But by hosting their e-commerce sites on cloud computing platforms, merchants can offload (4) ______ of the server processing work. These third-party systems still (5) ______ full control over the look and feel of their online stores.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. terms.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "In terms of" is a fixed idiomatic phrase meaning "with respect to" or "regarding", commonly used before listing specific aspects or measures of something (here, shipping costs and fulfillment times).

• "That convenience comes with a cost in terms of shipping costs and order fulfillment times" is the natural, idiomatic reading of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "firms" refers to companies/businesses; "a cost in firms of" is meaningless.

• Option 3: "shifts" refers to changes or work periods; "a cost in shifts of" does not fit the phrase idiomatically.

• Option 4: "tags" refers to labels; "a cost in tags of" does not make sense.

NOTE

• "In terms of" is a very frequently tested fixed phrase in SSC cloze passages, always followed by a noun/noun phrase specifying the aspect being discussed.

• Similar fixed phrases: "in view of", "in light of", "in spite of", "in case of".

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.
First, the e-commerce industry has historically struggled with (1)______ issues. The Internet has made it possible for customers to place (2) ______ from any location, but that convenience comes with a cost in (3) ______ of shipping costs and order fulfillment times. But by hosting their e-commerce sites on cloud computing platforms, merchants can offload (4) ______ of the server processing work. These third-party systems still (5) ______ full control over the look and feel of their online stores.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. much.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Work" here is an uncountable noun, so it must be quantified using an uncountable quantifier such as "much", not a countable quantifier like "many".

• "Merchants can offload much of the server processing work" correctly expresses that a large, unspecified amount (not a specific count) of the workload is transferred.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "must" is a modal verb expressing obligation and cannot grammatically follow "offload" in this position ("offload must of" is meaningless).

• Option 3: "many" is used with countable nouns, but "work" here is uncountable, so "many of the...work" is grammatically incorrect.

• Option 4: "more" would need a point of comparison ("more...than") which is absent here, making it contextually less precise than "much".

NOTE

• Countable vs uncountable quantifiers: use "many/few" with countable nouns (e.g., many orders), and "much/little" with uncountable nouns (e.g., much work, much information).

• Common SSC trap: confusing "many" and "much" based on whether the noun that follows them is countable or uncountable.

question:
Comprehension:

In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.
First, the e-commerce industry has historically struggled with (1)______ issues. The Internet has made it possible for customers to place (2) ______ from any location, but that convenience comes with a cost in (3) ______ of shipping costs and order fulfillment times. But by hosting their e-commerce sites on cloud computing platforms, merchants can offload (4) ______ of the server processing work. These third-party systems still (5) ______ full control over the look and feel of their online stores.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. retain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Retain" means to continue to have or keep something; "retain full control" means to keep complete control over something despite outsourcing other tasks.

• The sentence explains that although merchants offload server processing work to third-party cloud platforms, their own e-commerce systems still keep — retain — full control over the design, i.e. the "look and feel", of their online stores, rather than the third-party host dictating it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "placate" means to soothe or calm someone's anger; it does not fit with "control" as its object in this way.

• Option 2: "fumigate" means to disinfect with fumes or smoke; entirely unrelated to the context of control over a website's design.

• Option 4: "discard" means to get rid of or throw away; this is the opposite of what the sentence intends, since the merchants keep control rather than give it up.

NOTE

• "Retain control/possession/ownership" is a common fixed collocation tested in SSC cloze/vocabulary questions.

• Antonym pair to remember: retain (to keep) x discard/relinquish (to give up).
